notes.front: What does it mean to ground (earth) a piece of equipment?
notes.back: To connect it, by a conductive connection, to reference ground: the conductive body, usually earth, to which voltages are referenced.
notes.explanation: An effective ground has low enough impedance to stop voltages building up that could endanger people or equipment.
notes.example: A tower connected to a rod driven into the soil is grounded to earth.

notes.front: What is bonding, in electrical safety?
notes.back: Deliberately connecting metal parts together so that the potential differences between them are kept to a minimum.
notes.explanation: A bonded path must be able to carry safely any current likely to be imposed on it; the bonded group can then be connected to ground.
notes.example: Joining all of a station's ground rods together with heavy wire or strap.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1910.268(s)(7) (“Bond”); 29 CFR 1910.399 (“Bonding”); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0A09

notes.front: In US AC wiring, what is the hot conductor?
notes.back: The conductor with significant voltage to Earth, as opposed to the neutral, which stays near ground potential.
notes.explanation: The hot conductor is the one that can deliver a shock, which is why protective devices are placed in it.
notes.example: In standard US cable, black insulation marks the hot, white the neutral, and bare or green the safety ground.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Electrical wiring in North America”, section “Wiring methods”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · US colour convention as described on Wikipedia

notes.front: What is a fuse?
notes.back: A safety device with a metal wire or strip that melts when too much current flows, breaking the circuit.
notes.explanation: It protects against overcurrent, and once it has blown it must be replaced.
notes.example: Like a deliberately weak link in a chain, built to break first and save everything else.

notes.front: What is a circuit breaker?
notes.back: A device that opens a circuit automatically on overcurrent without damage to itself, and can be closed again by hand.
notes.explanation: It does a fuse’s job, protecting equipment and preventing fire, but is reset rather than replaced.
notes.example: Like a fuse you can switch back on after it trips.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1910.399 (“Circuit breaker”); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0A05, T0A08

notes.front: What is a lightning arrester?
notes.back: A device on a line that protects the system’s insulation from lightning by carrying the surge away, usually to earth.
notes.explanation: In a station it goes on a grounded panel where the feed lines enter the building, so a surge coming down the coax is sent to ground before it gets inside.
notes.example: Like a pressure-relief valve on a boiler: idle until a surge arrives, then it dumps it safely.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1910.269, Appendix B (“Surge arresters”); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0A07; Wikipedia, “Lightning arrester”

notes.front: What is a filter (smoothing) capacitor in a power supply?
notes.back: A capacitor after the rectifier that smooths its output into steady DC.
notes.explanation: Like any capacitor it stores charge, which is why the pool warns it can hold a hazardous charge after the supply is off.
notes.example: Like a water tank after a pulsing pump: it keeps the pressure steady, and stays full after the pump stops.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Rectifier”, section “Rectifier output smoothing”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0A11

notes.front: What is a guy line on an antenna tower or mast?
notes.back: A cable from a mast or tower to an anchor in the ground, tensioned to hold the structure steady.
notes.explanation: Masts are usually supported by guys, and extra guy wires and anchor stakes strengthen an antenna against heavy ice and wind; their tension is set with turnbuckles.
notes.example: Like the guy ropes that hold up a tent pole.
notes.source: US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 7-2; US Army, TM 11-666, Antennas and Radio Propagation (1953), para 77; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0B05

notes.front: What is a turnbuckle?
notes.back: A threaded device for adjusting a cable's tension: turning its frame screws both ends in or out together.
notes.explanation: On a tower it sets the tension of each guy line, so it must not work loose.
notes.example: Like a tent's tension slider, but a metal frame with a right-hand thread at one end and a left-hand thread at the other.

notes.front: What is ionizing radiation?
notes.back: Particles or electromagnetic waves with enough energy to knock electrons off atoms or molecules.
notes.explanation: Gamma rays from radioactive material are ionizing, and so are X-rays and the higher-energy part of ultraviolet; radio signals are not.
notes.example: Gamma rays from radioactive material are ionizing radiation.

notes.front: What is non-ionizing radiation?
notes.back: Electromagnetic radiation without enough energy to knock electrons off atoms or molecules (ionize them).
notes.explanation: Radio signals are non-ionizing: they lack the energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA.
notes.example: Radio broadcasting and telecommunications use non-ionizing radiation; gamma rays, by contrast, are ionizing.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Non-ionizing radiation” (lead section); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0C12

notes.front: In the FCC's RF exposure limits, what is power density and what unit is it given in?
notes.back: The RF power reaching a given area, in milliwatts per square centimetre (mW/cm²).
notes.explanation: It is the quantity the exposure tables list for every frequency range, so a lower allowed figure means a stricter limit.
notes.example: 0.2 mW/cm² is the general-population limit from 30 to 300 MHz.

notes.front: What is maximum permissible exposure (MPE)?
notes.back: The FCC's limits on RF field strength and power density that people may be exposed to, set range by range by frequency.
notes.explanation: Table 1 of 47 CFR 1.1310 lists separate MPE limits for occupational (controlled) and general-population (uncontrolled) exposure.
notes.example: The occupational MPE from 30 to 300 MHz is 1.0 mW/cm²; the general-population MPE is 0.2 mW/cm².

notes.front: What is the averaging time in the FCC's MPE limits?
notes.back: The period over which exposure may be averaged: 6 minutes for occupational limits, 30 minutes for general-population limits.
notes.explanation: Exposure above the limit is allowed for shorter times, as long as the average over this period stays within it (1.1310(d)(4)).
notes.example: Like a speed limit judged on your average over a stretch of road, not at one instant.

notes.front: What is duty cycle, for RF exposure?
notes.back: The percentage of time a transmitter is transmitting during the averaging time.
notes.explanation: A lower duty cycle lowers the average exposure, so a higher power density is allowed.
notes.example: Transmitting for 15 minutes of a 30-minute averaging time is a 50% duty cycle.

notes.front: What is FCC OET Bulletin 65?
notes.back: The FCC's guide “Evaluating Compliance with FCC Guidelines for Human Exposure to Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Fields”.
notes.explanation: Part 97 points licensees to it, and to its Supplement B for amateur stations, for how to evaluate a station's RF exposure.
notes.example: A licensee can calculate expected exposure in a neighbour's garden using its methods.

notes.front: What can happen if you short the terminals of a 12 V storage battery that has no internal protection circuitry?
notes.back: Burns, fire or an explosion.
notes.explanation: A short lets excessive current flow, and excessive current can cause a fire; a battery without protection circuitry has nothing to limit it.

notes.front: What hazard exists when an unprotected battery is charged or discharged rapidly?
notes.back: Overheating or out-gassing.
notes.explanation: Out-gassing means the battery gives off gas. Charging or discharging rapidly drives a large current through the battery, and an unprotected battery has no circuit to limit it.

notes.front: What three harms can electrical current through the body cause?
notes.back: Heating of body tissue; disruption of cells' electrical functions; involuntary muscle contractions.
notes.explanation: Each is a separate injury, so the pool keys all three: heat damages tissue, disrupted cell function upsets the body’s own electrical signals, and involuntary contractions take away control of your muscles.

notes.front: What three ways does the pool give to guard against electrical shock at your station?
notes.back: Three-wire cords and plugs; a common safety ground for AC equipment; discharging high-voltage DC capacitors before working inside.
notes.explanation: Each removes a route to a shock: three-wire cords and a common safety ground give fault current a safe path to ground, and discharging capacitors removes charge they can hold after the power is off.

notes.front: In the US, what does black insulation indicate in a three-wire 120 V AC cable?
notes.back: The hot conductor.
notes.explanation: White marks the neutral and bare or green the safety ground, so the black wire is the one carrying dangerous voltage.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0A03; Wikipedia, “Electrical wiring in North America”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · US colour convention as described on Wikipedia

notes.front: Where should a fuse or circuit breaker be installed in a 120 V AC power circuit?
notes.back: In series with the hot conductor only.
notes.explanation: In series, all the current passes through it; on the hot side, blowing it removes the dangerous voltage from the equipment.

notes.front: What is the purpose of a fuse in an electrical circuit, according to the pool?
notes.back: To remove power in case of an overload.
notes.explanation: It melts and breaks the circuit when too much current flows.

notes.front: Why must a 5 A fuse never be replaced with a 20 A fuse?
notes.back: Excessive current could flow and cause a fire.
notes.explanation: The circuit was designed for 5 A; a 20 A fuse would let four times that flow before blowing.

notes.front: Where should a lightning arrester be installed in a coaxial feed line?
notes.back: On a grounded panel near where the feed lines enter the building.
notes.explanation: That diverts a surge to ground before it reaches the station equipment inside.

notes.front: What should be done to all external ground rods or earth connections?
notes.back: Bond them together with heavy wire or conductive strap.
notes.explanation: Bonded rods sit at the same potential, so no dangerous voltage can build up between them.

notes.front: What is good practice for ground wires on a tower for lightning protection?
notes.back: Keep the connections short and direct.
notes.explanation: The pool rejects drip loops and right-angle bends; the path to ground should be as direct as possible.

notes.front: What must be avoided when installing grounding conductors for lightning protection?
notes.back: Sharp bends.
notes.explanation: This matches the pool: lightning ground connections should be short and direct.

notes.front: What hazard exists in a power supply immediately after it is turned off?
notes.back: Charge stored in the filter capacitors.
notes.explanation: Filter capacitors can hold a hazardous voltage after the supply is switched off, so discharge them before working inside.

notes.front: What precaution applies when measuring high voltages with a voltmeter?
notes.back: Make sure the voltmeter and its leads are rated for the voltages being measured.
notes.explanation: The meter and its leads are all that stand between your hands and the circuit; if they are not rated for the voltage, their insulation cannot be relied on to hold it off.

notes.front: What three things does the pool require when climbing an antenna tower?
notes.back: Sufficient training in safe climbing; tie-off to the tower at all times; an approved climbing harness.
notes.explanation: Each guards against a fall: training in safe technique, tie-off at all times, and an approved harness to tie off with.

notes.front: When is it safe to climb a tower without a helper or observer?
notes.back: Never.
notes.explanation: If you fall or are hurt on the tower, only someone on the ground can call for help; no height limit or type of work removes that risk.

notes.front: What important precaution applies when putting up an antenna tower?
notes.back: Look for, and stay clear of, any overhead electrical wires.
notes.explanation: Contact with power lines is the danger; the pool rejects wrist ground straps and insulating the tower base.

notes.front: What is the purpose of a safety wire through a turnbuckle on a guy line?
notes.back: To stop the turnbuckle loosening from vibration.
notes.explanation: A turnbuckle that turns loose lets the guy line lose tension.

notes.front: When may a crank-up tower be climbed?
notes.back: Only when it is retracted, or mechanical safety locking devices have been installed.
notes.explanation: The rule is about when the tower can safely take a climber’s weight: fully retracted, or extended only with mechanical safety locks fitted to hold the sections in place.

notes.front: What is a proper grounding method for a tower?
notes.back: Separate eight-foot ground rods for each tower leg, bonded to the tower and to each other.
notes.explanation: The pool rejects a single four-foot rod, an RF choke and a cold-water pipe.

notes.front: What sets the grounding requirements for an amateur radio tower or antenna?
notes.back: Local electrical codes.
notes.explanation: Grounding is a matter for local electrical codes, not the FCC’s Part 97 rules, aviation (FAA) tower-lighting rules or a private safety-standards organisation’s (UL) practices.

notes.front: What is the minimum safe distance from a power line when installing an antenna?
notes.back: Far enough that if the antenna falls, no part of it can come within 10 feet of the power wires.
notes.explanation: The distance is judged by where the antenna could land if it falls, not by a formula or a wavelength.

notes.front: Why should you avoid attaching an antenna to a utility pole?
notes.back: The antenna could contact high-voltage power lines.
notes.explanation: The danger is contact with the power lines, not any effect on the antenna's performance.

notes.front: What type of radiation are radio signals?
notes.back: Non-ionizing radiation.
notes.explanation: Radio signals do not have enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, unlike gamma rays or the alpha particles given off by radioactive material.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0C01; Wikipedia, “Ionizing radiation”

notes.front: How does RF radiation differ from ionizing radiation (radioactivity)?
notes.back: RF radiation lacks the energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA.
notes.explanation: That does not make it perfectly safe: touching a transmitting antenna can cause an RF burn.

notes.front: Why do RF exposure limits vary with frequency?
notes.back: The human body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others.
notes.explanation: Limits are strictest where absorption is greatest, which for the general population is 30–300 MHz in 47 CFR 1.1310.

notes.front: Which frequency range has the lowest general-population MPE power density limit, and what is it?
notes.back: 30–300 MHz: 0.2 mW/cm², averaged over 30 minutes.
notes.explanation: Below 30 MHz and above 300 MHz the limit rises; from 1500 MHz upwards it is 1.0 mW/cm².

image.alt: Step chart of the FCC general-population MPE power density limit against frequency, both on log scales: 100 mW/cm² from 0.3 to 1.34 MHz, falling as 180/f² to 0.2 mW/cm² at 30 MHz, flat at 0.2 from 30 to 300 MHz, rising as f/1500 to 1.0 at 1500 MHz, then flat at 1.0 up to 100,000 MHz. Marked points: 3.5 MHz about 14.7, 50 MHz 0.2, 440 MHz about 0.29, 1296 MHz about 0.86 mW/cm².
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from 47 CFR 1.1310(e)(1), Table 1

notes.front: How does the allowable power density change if duty cycle falls from 100% to 50%?
notes.back: It doubles (increases by a factor of 2).
notes.explanation: Transmitting half the time halves the average exposure, so twice the power density is allowed.

notes.front: Why is duty cycle one of the factors in safe RF exposure levels?
notes.back: It affects the average exposure to radiation.
notes.explanation: Exposure limits are averaged over time, so how much of that time you transmit matters.

notes.front: What three factors affect the RF exposure of people near an amateur antenna?
notes.back: The RF field's frequency and power level; the distance from the antenna; the antenna's radiation pattern.
notes.explanation: Each changes how much RF reaches a person: more power, a closer person or a pattern aimed at them all raise exposure, and the body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others.

notes.front: What three methods can show that your station complies with FCC RF exposure rules?
notes.back: Calculation based on OET Bulletin 65; calculation by computer modelling; field-strength measurement with calibrated equipment.
notes.explanation: Any of the three can show whether the fields people receive stay within the FCC limits; the rules require the licensee to act before transmitting from a place where exposure could exceed them.

notes.front: How do you keep your station compliant with RF safety rules over time?
notes.back: Re-evaluate it whenever an item in the transmitter or antenna system is changed.
notes.explanation: A change of power, antenna or position can change exposure, so the earlier evaluation may no longer hold.

notes.front: Which action from the pool reduces exposure to RF radiation?
notes.back: Relocating the antennas.
notes.explanation: Exposure depends on distance from the antenna; moving the transmitter does not move the radiating antenna.

notes.front: What hazard is created by touching an antenna during a transmission?
notes.back: An RF burn to the skin.
notes.explanation: RF is non-ionizing, so the danger is a burn, not ionizing radiation.

notes.front: Who is responsible for ensuring that no one is exposed to RF energy above the FCC limits?
notes.back: The station licensee.
notes.explanation: Part 97 requires the licensee to ensure compliance and, if limits could be exceeded in accessible areas, to act to prevent exposure (97.13(c)).

notes.front: Which exposure limits may an amateur use to evaluate members of their own household?
notes.back: The occupational/controlled limits, provided the licensee and household have had appropriate training and information.
notes.explanation: Other nearby people who are not household members must be evaluated against the general-population/uncontrolled limits.

notes.front: Which of the following is a safety hazard of a 12-volt storage battery that lacks internal protection circuitry?
notes.back: Shorting the terminals can cause burns, fire, or an explosion
notes.choices:
A) Touching both terminals with your hands can cause electrical shock
B) Shorting the terminals can cause burns, fire, or an explosion
C) RF emissions from a nearby transmitter can cause the electrolyte to emit poison gas
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pool keys the short circuit, not touching the terminals, as the hazard of a 12 V battery. C: the pool keys no RF effect on the electrolyte; the hazard is the short circuit. D: A and C are wrong, so not all choices are correct.
notes.explanation: A short lets excessive current flow, and excessive current can cause a fire; a battery without protection circuitry has nothing to limit it.

notes.front: What health hazard is posed by electrical current flowing through the body?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) It may cause injury by heating body tissue
B) It may disrupt the electrical functions of cells
C) It may cause involuntary muscle contractions
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each is a real harm, so none alone is the full answer.
notes.explanation: Current through the body can heat tissue, disrupt the electrical functions of cells and cause involuntary muscle contractions.

notes.front: In the United States, what circuit does black wire insulation indicate in a three-wire 120 V AC cable?
notes.back: Hot
notes.choices:
A) Neutral
B) Hot
C) Equipment ground
D) Negative
notes.choicesExplained: A: the neutral is white. C: the equipment ground is bare or green. D: “negative” is a DC term; AC wiring has hot and neutral.
notes.explanation: In a US three-wire 120 V AC cable, black insulation marks the hot conductor; white is the neutral and bare or green the ground.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0A03; Wikipedia, “Electrical wiring in North America”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · US colour convention as described on Wikipedia

notes.front: What is the purpose of a fuse in an electrical circuit?
notes.back: To remove power in case of an overload
notes.choices:
A) To prevent power supply ripple from damaging a component
B) To remove power in case of an overload
C) To limit current and prevent shocks
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: ripple is smoothed by filter capacitors, not by a fuse. C: a fuse does not limit current to prevent shocks; it only opens on overload. D: A and C are wrong.
notes.explanation: A fuse melts and breaks the circuit when too much current flows, removing power in case of an overload.

notes.front: Why should a 5-ampere fuse never be replaced with a 20-ampere fuse?
notes.back: Excessive current could cause a fire
notes.choices:
A) The larger fuse would be likely to blow because it is rated for higher current
B) The power supply ripple would greatly increase
C) Excessive current could cause a fire
D) Voltage drop in the higher current fuse could result in excessively low voltage to the device
notes.choicesExplained: A: a higher-rated fuse is less likely to blow, not more. B: a fuse has nothing to do with power supply ripple. D: the danger is too much current, not too little voltage.
notes.explanation: A 20 A fuse lets up to four times the designed current flow before it blows, and that excess current could cause a fire.

notes.front: What is a good way to guard against electrical shock at your station?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Use three-wire cords and plugs for all AC powered equipment
B) Connect all AC powered station equipment to a common safety ground
C) Ensure all capacitors used for high-voltage DC are fully discharged before working inside equipment
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each is a recommended precaution, so none alone is the full answer.
notes.explanation: Three-wire cords, a common safety ground and discharging high-voltage capacitors before working inside all guard against shock.

notes.front: Where should a lightning arrester be installed in a coaxial feed line?
notes.back: On a grounded panel near where feed lines enter the building
notes.choices:
A) At the output connector of a transceiver
B) At the antenna feed point
C) At the AC power service panel
D) On a grounded panel near where feed lines enter the building
notes.choicesExplained: A: at the transceiver the surge has already entered the building. B: at the feed point the surge still travels down the whole line into the building. C: the AC service panel is on the power wiring, not in the coaxial feed line.
notes.explanation: Mounted on a grounded panel near the building entry, the arrester diverts a surge on the feed line to ground before it reaches the equipment.

notes.front: Where should a fuse or circuit breaker be installed in a 120V AC power circuit?
notes.back: In series with the hot conductor only
notes.choices:
A) In series with the hot conductor only
B) In series with the hot and neutral conductors
C) In parallel with the hot conductor only
D) In parallel with the hot and neutral conductors
notes.choicesExplained: B: a fuse in the neutral could blow and leave the equipment still connected to the hot conductor, which carries the dangerous voltage. C and D: a device in parallel does not carry the circuit’s current, so it could not interrupt it.
notes.explanation: In series with the hot conductor, the fuse or breaker carries all the circuit's current, and opening it disconnects the dangerous voltage.

notes.front: What should be done to all external ground rods or earth connections?
notes.back: Bond them together with heavy wire or conductive strap
notes.choices:
A) Waterproof them with silicone caulk or electrical tape
B) Keep them as far apart as possible
C) Bond them together with heavy wire or conductive strap
D) Tune them for resonance on the lowest frequency of operation
notes.choicesExplained: A: waterproofing does not connect the rods to each other. B: separation without bonding lets a voltage build up between them. D: ground rods are not tuned for resonance.
notes.explanation: Bonding all ground rods together with heavy wire or strap keeps them at the same potential.

notes.front: What hazard exists when rapidly charging or discharging an unprotected battery?
notes.back: Overheating or out-gassing
notes.choices:
A) Overheating or out-gassing
B) Excess output ripple
C) Electric shock
D) Overvoltage
notes.choicesExplained: B: ripple is a power supply property, not a battery hazard. C: the pool keys heat and gas, not shock. D: the hazard keyed is overheating or out-gassing, not overvoltage.
notes.explanation: Rapid charging or discharging of an unprotected battery can make it overheat or give off gas.

notes.front: What hazard exists in a power supply immediately after turning it off?
notes.back: Charge stored in filter capacitors
notes.choices:
A) Circulating currents in the dc filter
B) Leakage flux in the power transformer
C) Voltage transients from kickback diodes
D) Charge stored in filter capacitors
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: none of these lasts once the supply is switched off; the charge stored in the filter capacitors does.
notes.explanation: Filter capacitors store charge and can keep a dangerous voltage after the supply is switched off.

notes.front: Which of the following precautions should be taken when measuring high voltages with a voltmeter?
notes.back: Ensure that the voltmeter and its leads are rated for use at the voltages being measured
notes.choices:
A) Ensure that the voltmeter has very low impedance
B) Ensure that the voltmeter and its leads are rated for use at the voltages being measured
C) Ensure that the circuit is grounded through the voltmeter
D) Ensure that the voltmeter is set to the correct frequency
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: none protects you from the voltage: impedance and a frequency setting say nothing about insulation, and a meter must never be the circuit’s path to ground. Only a meter and leads rated for the voltage are safe to use on it.
notes.explanation: The meter and its leads are all that stand between your hands and the circuit, so they must be rated for the voltages being measured.

notes.front: Which of the following is good practice when installing ground wires on a tower for lightning protection?
notes.back: Ensure that connections are short and direct
notes.choices:
A) Put a drip loop in the ground connection to prevent water damage to the ground system
B) Make sure all ground wire bends are right angles
C) Ensure that connections are short and direct
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pool does not recommend a drip loop in the ground connection. B: right-angle bends are to be avoided. D: A and B are wrong.
notes.explanation: Short, direct ground connections give lightning the easiest path to earth.

notes.front: What is required when climbing an antenna tower?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Have sufficient training on safe tower climbing techniques
B) Use appropriate tie-off to the tower at all times
C) Always wear an approved climbing harness
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each is required, so none alone is the full answer.
notes.explanation: Training, constant tie-off and an approved harness are all required when climbing a tower.

notes.front: Under what circumstances is it safe to climb a tower without a helper or observer?
notes.back: Never
notes.choices:
A) When no electrical work is being performed
B) When no mechanical work is being performed
C) When the work being done is not more than 20 feet above the ground
D) Never
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: no kind of work or height limit makes climbing alone safe.
notes.explanation: A helper or observer is always needed when climbing a tower.

notes.front: Which of the following is an important safety precaution to observe when putting up an antenna tower?
notes.back: Look for and stay clear of any overhead electrical wires
notes.choices:
A) Wear a ground strap connected to your wrist at all times
B) Insulate the base of the tower to avoid lightning strikes
C) Look for and stay clear of any overhead electrical wires
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: a wrist ground strap is not the precaution the pool keys; the danger is overhead power wires. B: the tower must be grounded, not insulated. D: A and B are wrong.
notes.explanation: Overhead electrical wires are the key hazard when raising a tower; look for them and stay clear.

notes.front: What is the purpose of a safety wire through a turnbuckle used to tension guy lines?
notes.back: Prevent loosening of the turnbuckle from vibration
notes.choices:
A) Secure the guy line if the turnbuckle breaks
B) Prevent loosening of the turnbuckle from vibration
C) Provide a ground path for lightning strikes
D) Provide an ability to measure for proper tensioning
notes.choicesExplained: A: the wire does not hold the guy if the turnbuckle breaks. C: it is not a lightning ground path. D: it is not a tension gauge.
notes.explanation: A safety wire through the turnbuckle stops vibration from gradually unscrewing it and loosening the guy line.

notes.front: What is the minimum safe distance from a power line to allow when installing an antenna?
notes.back: Enough so that if the antenna falls, no part of it can come within 10 feet of the power wires
notes.choices:
A) Add the height of the antenna to the height of the power line and multiply by a factor of 1.5
B) The height of the power line above ground
C) 1/2 wavelength at the operating frequency
D) Enough so that if the antenna falls, no part of it can come within 10 feet of the power wires
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pool uses no 1.5 factor. B: the power line's height alone ignores how far the antenna could fall. C: wavelength has nothing to do with safety clearance.
notes.explanation: If the antenna falls, a 10-foot margin keeps every part of it clear of the power wires; contact with high-voltage lines puts that voltage on the antenna and anyone touching it.

notes.front: Which of the following is an important safety rule to remember when using a crank-up tower?
notes.back: This type of tower must not be climbed unless it is retracted, or mechanical safety locking devices have been installed
notes.choices:
A) This type of tower must never be painted
B) This type of tower must never be grounded
C) This type of tower must not be climbed unless it is retracted, or mechanical safety locking devices have been installed
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pool has no rule against painting it. B: towers must be grounded. D: A and B are wrong.
notes.explanation: The rule is about when the tower can safely take a climber’s weight: fully retracted, or extended only with mechanical safety locks fitted to hold the sections in place.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0B07, T0B08, T0B11

notes.front: Which is a proper grounding method for a tower?
notes.back: Separate eight-foot ground rods for each tower leg, bonded to the tower and each other
notes.choices:
A) A single four-foot ground rod, driven into the ground no more than 12 inches from the base
B) A ferrite-core RF choke connected between the tower and ground
C) A connection between the tower base and a cold-water pipe
D) Separate eight-foot ground rods for each tower leg, bonded to the tower and each other
notes.choicesExplained: A: a single short rod is less than the keyed separate eight-foot rods on every leg, bonded together. B: an RF choke blocks RF; it is not a ground connection. C: a cold-water pipe is not the keyed tower ground; rods at each leg, bonded to the tower and each other, are.
notes.explanation: Each tower leg gets its own eight-foot ground rod, and all are bonded to the tower and to each other.

notes.front: Why should you avoid attaching an antenna to a utility pole?
notes.back: The antenna could contact high-voltage power lines
notes.choices:
A) The antenna will not work properly because of induced voltages
B) The antenna may unbalance the power transformer, causing power fluctuations
C) The antenna could contact high-voltage power lines
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the concern is safety, not antenna performance or the power transformer. D: A and B are wrong.
notes.explanation: Utility poles carry high-voltage power lines; an antenna touching one would put that voltage on the antenna, its cable and anyone touching them.

notes.front: Which of the following is true when installing grounding conductors used for lightning protection?
notes.back: Sharp bends must be avoided
notes.choices:
A) Use only non-insulated wire
B) Wires must be carefully routed with precise right-angle bends
C) Sharp bends must be avoided
D) Common grounds must be avoided
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pool does not require non-insulated wire. B: precise right-angle bends are exactly what to avoid. D: grounds are to be bonded together, not kept apart.
notes.explanation: Lightning grounding conductors must avoid sharp bends, keeping the path short and direct.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0B10, T0B01, T0A09

notes.front: Which of the following establishes grounding requirements for an amateur radio tower or antenna?
notes.back: Local electrical codes
notes.choices:
A) FCC Part 97 rules
B) Local electrical codes
C) FAA tower lighting regulations
D) UL recommended practices
notes.choicesExplained: A: Part 97 does not set tower grounding rules. C: FAA rules concern tower lighting, not grounding. D: UL practices are not the governing rule the pool keys.
notes.explanation: Grounding is a matter for local electrical codes, not the FCC’s Part 97 rules, aviation (FAA) tower-lighting rules or a private safety-standards organisation’s (UL) practices.

notes.front: What type of radiation are radio signals?
notes.back: Non-ionizing radiation
notes.choices:
A) Gamma radiation
B) Ionizing radiation
C) Alpha radiation
D) Non-ionizing radiation
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: gamma and alpha radiation come from radioactivity and are ionizing. B: radio signals are the opposite of ionizing radiation.
notes.explanation: Radio signals are non-ionizing: they lack the energy to ionize atoms or molecules.

notes.front: Which of the following bands has the lowest maximum permissible exposure for RF safety?
notes.back: 50 MHz
notes.choices:
A) 3.5 MHz
B) 50 MHz
C) 440 MHz
D) 1296 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: at 3.5 MHz the general-population limit is 180/f², about 14.7 mW/cm². C: at 440 MHz it is f/1500, about 0.29 mW/cm². D: at 1296 MHz it is about 0.86 mW/cm².
notes.explanation: 50 MHz falls in 30–300 MHz, the range with the lowest limit: 0.2 mW/cm² for the general population (47 CFR 1.1310, Table 1).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0C02; 47 CFR 1.1310(e)(1), Table 1

notes.front: How does the allowable power density for RF safety change if duty cycle changes from 100 percent to 50 percent?
notes.back: It increases by a factor of 2
notes.choices:
A) It increases by a factor of 3
B) It decreases by 50 percent
C) It increases by a factor of 2
D) There is no adjustment allowed for lower duty cycle
notes.choicesExplained: A: the factor is 2, not 3. B: allowable power density rises, not falls. D: duty cycle is allowed for, because limits are averaged over time.
notes.explanation: Halving the duty cycle halves the average exposure, so the allowable power density doubles.

notes.front: What factors affect the RF exposure of people near an amateur station antenna?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Frequency and power level of the RF field
B) Distance from the antenna to a person
C) Radiation pattern of the antenna
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each is a factor, so none alone is the full answer.
notes.explanation: Frequency and power level, distance from the antenna and the antenna's radiation pattern all affect exposure.

notes.front: Why do exposure limits vary with frequency?
notes.back: The human body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others
notes.choices:
A) Lower frequency RF fields have more energy than higher frequency fields
B) Lower frequency RF fields do not penetrate the human body
C) Higher frequency RF fields are transient in nature
D) The human body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others
notes.choicesExplained: A: RF at any frequency lacks the energy to cause chemical changes in cells; limits vary with how much the body absorbs. B: the body does absorb RF energy, more at some frequencies than others. C: RF fields are not “transient” by nature.
notes.explanation: The body absorbs RF energy more at some frequencies than others, so limits are strictest where absorption is greatest.

notes.front: Which of the following is an acceptable method to determine whether your station complies with FCC RF exposure regulations?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) By calculation based on FCC OET Bulletin 65
B) By calculation based on computer modeling
C) By measurement of field strength using calibrated equipment
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each is acceptable, so none alone is the full answer.
notes.explanation: Calculation per OET Bulletin 65, computer modelling and calibrated field-strength measurement are all acceptable.

notes.front: What hazard is created by touching an antenna during a transmission?
notes.back: RF burn to skin
notes.choices:
A) Electrocution
B) RF burn to skin
C) Exposure to ionizing radiation
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pool keys an RF burn, not electrocution. C: RF is non-ionizing. D: A and C are wrong.
notes.explanation: RF current flows into your skin where you touch the antenna; RF is non-ionizing, so the harm is a burn, not radiation damage to cells.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0C07, T0C01, T0C12

notes.front: Which of the following actions can reduce exposure to RF radiation?
notes.back: Relocate antennas
notes.choices:
A) Relocate antennas
B) Relocate the transmitter
C) Increase the duty cycle
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B: the antenna, not the transmitter, radiates. C: a higher duty cycle increases average exposure. D: B and C are wrong.
notes.explanation: Moving the antennas increases the distance between them and people, reducing exposure.

notes.front: How can you make sure your station stays in compliance with RF safety regulations?
notes.back: By re-evaluating the station whenever an item in the transmitter or antenna system is changed
notes.choices:
A) By informing the FCC of any changes made in your station
B) By re-evaluating the station whenever an item in the transmitter or antenna system is changed
C) By making sure your antennas have low SWR
D) By using only Underwriter Laboratories approved transmitting equipment
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pool's answer is to re-evaluate, not to inform the FCC. C: SWR measures how well the load matches the feed line, not exposure. D: equipment approval does not evaluate exposure at your station.
notes.explanation: Any change to the transmitter or antenna system can change exposure, so re-evaluate the station after each one.

notes.front: Why is duty cycle one of the factors used to determine safe RF radiation exposure levels?
notes.back: It affects the average exposure to radiation
notes.choices:
A) It affects the average exposure to radiation
B) It affects the peak exposure to radiation
C) It takes into account the antenna feed line loss
D) It takes into account the thermal effects of the final amplifier
notes.choicesExplained: B: the limits concern average, not peak, exposure. C and D: duty cycle has nothing to do with feed line loss or the amplifier's heat.
notes.explanation: Exposure limits are averaged over time, and duty cycle sets how much of that time you transmit, so it affects average exposure.

notes.front: What is the definition of duty cycle during the averaging time for RF exposure?
notes.back: The percentage of time that a transmitter is transmitting
notes.choices:
A) The difference between the lowest and highest power output of a transmitter
B) The difference between the PEP and the average power output of a transmitter
C) The percentage of time that a transmitter is transmitting
D) The percentage of time that a transmitter is not transmitting
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: these compare power levels, not time. D: this is the percentage of time not transmitting, the reverse.
notes.explanation: Exposure limits are averaged over a set time, so the share of that time you spend transmitting sets your average exposure.

notes.front: How does RF radiation differ from ionizing radiation (radioactivity)?
notes.back: RF radiation does not have sufficient energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA
notes.choices:
A) RF radiation does not have sufficient energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA
B) RF radiation can only be detected with an RF dosimeter
C) RF radiation is limited in range to a few feet
D) RF radiation is perfectly safe
notes.choicesExplained: B: detection is not the difference the pool keys; the difference is energy. C: radio signals travel far beyond a few feet. D: RF is not perfectly safe: it can cause burns.
notes.explanation: Radioactivity can cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA; RF lacks the energy for that, though it can still cause burns.

notes.front: Who is responsible for ensuring that no person is exposed to RF energy above the FCC exposure limits?
notes.back: The station licensee
notes.choices:
A) The FCC
B) The station licensee
C) Anyone who is near an antenna
D) The local zoning board
notes.choicesExplained: A: the FCC sets the limits, but 97.13(c) puts the duty on the licensee. C: people near an antenna are the ones protected. D: zoning boards do not set RF exposure duties.
notes.explanation: The station licensee must ensure compliance with the RF exposure limits and act if they could be exceeded (47 CFR 97.13(c)).

notes.front: Gamma rays versus radio signals: which is ionizing radiation, and what is the difference?
notes.back: Gamma rays are ionizing; radio signals are non-ionizing, lacking the energy to ionize atoms or damage DNA.
notes.explanation: Non-ionizing does not mean harmless: RF can still cause burns, which is why exposure limits exist.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Ionizing radiation” and “Non-ionizing radiation” (lead sections); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0C12

notes.front: Fuse versus circuit breaker: what happens to each after it interrupts an overcurrent?
notes.back: A fuse has melted and must be replaced; a circuit breaker can be reset.
notes.explanation: Both protect against too much current and go in series with the hot conductor.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1910.399 (“Fuse”, “Circuit breaker”); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T0A08

notes.front: From 30 to 300 MHz, how do the occupational/controlled and general-population/uncontrolled MPE limits differ?
notes.back: Occupational: 1.0 mW/cm² averaged over 6 minutes. General population: 0.2 mW/cm² averaged over 30 minutes.
notes.explanation: Occupational limits apply to people fully aware of the exposure and able to control it; everyone else gets the stricter general-population limits. (A trained licensee may also use occupational limits for their own household.)
